_meta: A weight, a small per-step optimizer update, and a step count, used to show why mixed-precision training must keep an fp32 MASTER copy of the weights: adding a tiny update directly to an fp16 weight underflows -- the update is smaller than the gap between representable fp16 values at that magnitude, so w + update rounds back to w and the step is lost, every step. This is separate from gradient underflow (which loss scaling fixes). Even with a perfectly good gradient, the optimizer's update to a weight is often minuscule relative to the weight itself -- a learning rate times a gradient can be thousands of times smaller than the weight it updates. fp16 has about 10 mantissa bits, so near a weight of magnitude 1 the smallest change it can represent (its ulp) is about 2^-10, roughly 0.001; an update of 0.0004 is below half that, so rounding w + update to the nearest fp16 value gives back w unchanged. The weight never moves and that parameter never learns. The fix is to hold the master weights in fp32, apply the update there where it accumulates faithfully, and round to fp16 only for the fast forward and backward passes: after enough steps the accumulated change in the master weight grows large enough to survive the fp16 rounding. weight is the starting weight; update is the per-step change the optimizer wants to apply; steps is how many steps; mantissa_bits sets the fp16 precision. These are the fixture; a single update's fate, the direct-fp16 weight after all steps, and the fp32-master weight after all steps are computed.
